The Revolt

Luigi Russolo paints a crowd in revolt as a red mass driving a row of repeated chevrons into a blue street, the clearest painted diagram of a Futurist line of force.

Context

Oil on canvas, 150.8 × 230.7 cm, c. 1911, made in Milan. Kunstmuseum Den Haag, object number 0333154, acquired from the Estate of Myrtil Frank and Flory Frank-Marburger. Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

Observed

  • Five or more red chevrons, each the same angle, repeat from the lower left toward the upper right, growing smaller and closer together.
  • The right half is a dense red-orange field with small scratched figures, the crowd, pushing into the angle of the chevrons.
  • Blue and violet buildings with dark square windows tilt away from the force, as if bent by it.
  • A yellow-green band runs between the red field and the buildings along the same diagonal.
  • Color is flat and nearly unmixed: red, orange, blue, yellow, green, and black.

Why it belongs

The repeated chevron is the Futurist idea of motion by repetition in its most graphic form. It works like a printed arrow and predicts the wedges of later poster design, including Lissitzky’s red wedge, although no direct link is documented here.

The painting is political: the force is a crowd, and the city bends before it.

Borrow

Repeat one wedge or chevron several times along a diagonal, closer together toward the target, to show direction and acceleration.

Let the shapes that receive the force tilt away from it.

Use one hot dominant field (red-orange) against a cool one (blue) with a narrow yellow band at the boundary.
